title: Εὔνουχος καὶ ἱερεύς
part: The Eunuch and the Priest (Chambry 113 · Perry 310)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 113 (= Perry 310). Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Εὔνουχος προσῆλθε ἱερεῖ, θυσίαν ὑπὲρ αὐτοῦ ποιῆσαι παρακαλῶν εἰς τὸ γενέσθαι παίδων πατέρα.
sentences.tr: Eunouchos prosēlthe hierei, thysian hyper autou poiēsai parakalōn eis to genesthai paidōn patera.
sentences.l: A eunuch came to a priest, calling upon him to perform a sacrifice on his behalf, toward his becoming a father of children.
sentences.i: A eunuch went to a priest and asked him to offer a sacrifice on his behalf, that he might become the father of children.
sentences.n: εἰς τὸ γενέσθαι is the articular infinitive after εἰς — the standard way Greek turns a whole action into a noun of purpose, 'toward the becoming'. The literal line keeps that shape; English prefers a clause. παρακαλῶ is 'summon, call upon, entreat', and it returns in the priest's answer.

sentences.t: Ὁ δὲ ἱερεὺς ἔφη· « Ὅτε μὲν πρὸς τὴν θυσίαν ἀπίδω, πατέρα σε γενέσθαι παίδων παρακαλῶ· ὅτε δὲ τὴν σὴν ὄψιν ἴδω, οὐδ’ ἀνὴρ φαίνῃ. »
sentences.tr: Ho de hiereus ephē· « Hote men pros tēn thysian apidō, patera se genesthai paidōn parakalō· hote de tēn sēn opsin idō, oud’ anēr phainēi. »
sentences.l: And the priest said: « When I look toward the sacrifice, I call upon you to become a father of children; but when I look at your appearance, you do not even seem a man. »
sentences.n: ὅτε with the subjunctive (ἀπίδω, ἴδω) and no ἄν: classical Attic prose would write ὅταν for this indefinite 'whenever'; the bare ὅτε is a later usage, and the sense is the same. παρακαλῶ takes the accusative and infinitive here (σε … γενέσθαι) — the same verb, and the same construction, that the eunuch used on him in the first line. ἀφοράω is to look away from everything else at one thing: the priest's eye rests on the offering, and moves to the man who brought it only afterwards. Chambry prints no moral for this fable.
